lesson.subtitle: Lesson 5 -- Holding the Floor
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Luiz Fernando da Silva | Lesson 5 -- Holding the Floor

listenings.text: I have covered elections for twenty-two years, and the question people ask me at dinners is always the same. How do you talk about politics with somebody who disagrees with you, without ruining the evening. My answer disappoints them, because it is not a clever technique. It is that you have to be genuinely curious about how the other person got there. Almost nobody arrives at a political position out of nowhere. They arrive at it through something that happened to them, or to their business, or to the town they grew up in. So the sentence that saves these conversations is not a counter-argument. It is: what would have to change for you to see it differently. And if I could give one more piece of advice, it would be this. Say where you are standing. From where I stand is an honest phrase, it costs nothing, and it turns a statement about the world into a statement about you, which is much harder to argue with and much more interesting to hear.

People think trade policy is an abstraction until it reaches a farm, and then it is extremely concrete. If a government changed the tariff on an imported input tomorrow, the farmer would not feel it tomorrow. He would feel it at planting, which might be four months later, and he would pay for it at harvest, which is another six. That delay is the whole difficulty of my job. I am asked to explain today a decision whose effect nobody will see for a year. What I have learned is to stop arguing about whether a policy is good, because that argument has no end, and to ask a narrower question instead. If this rule came into force in March, who would have to change what they are doing, and by when. Somebody always answers that one, and the room stops shouting. It is not that the disagreement disappears. It is that it becomes about dates and numbers, and dates and numbers can be checked.
